idiom_name: template literals and tagged templates in the render path
implementation_notes: In JavaScript the script form is the language's own interpolation: a template literal embeds expressions in markup, so an Express handler or a plain view function is the page, and a tag function (for example an html tag) can own escaping for the whole tree. The classic scriptlet engine (EJS) reproduces the same structure with <% %> for control flow and <%= %> for escaped output, and its documentation notes that EJS is effectively a JavaScript runtime, so it is only safe when the template text is trusted and data goes through the escaped tags. Native template literals remain justified for small server-rendered pages and email bodies; a real engine is the better home once templates must be editable outside the deploy.
pitfalls: ${expression} interpolates raw text: without an escape function or a tag function, injected markup is parsed by the browser - the scriptlet hazard in native syntax.
EJS's <%-> writes unescaped output next to <%= which escapes; that one-character difference is a common injection bug when templates are edited quickly.
Building the page by concatenating inside a loop allocates a new string per iteration; push fragments into an array and join once, or stream, for large pages.
Server-rendered strings that are later hydrated on the client must escape </script> sequences and stay byte-identical to what the client expects, or hydration mismatches corrupt the page.
